sections.facts: The Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act (XXIV of 1946) came into force on 19th November, 1946. By a notification of 14th December, 1946, under section 92(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Governor of Bengal directed that the Act shall apply to the District of Darjeeling, which was an 'excluded area'. Section 1(3) of the Act provided that it would cease to have effect upon the expiration of the period mentioned in section 4 of the India (Central Government and Legislature) Act, 1946. The operation of the Act was extended up to 31st March, 1948, by a notification issued by the Governor General, and subsequently extended up to 31st March, 1950, by resolutions passed by the Constituent Assembly, in which the powers of the Houses of Parliament had become vested following the Indian Independence Act, 1947. The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Act in respect of an act committed on 14th October, 1949, within Darjeeling.
sections.statute: Section 1(3) and Section 7 of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act (XXIV of 1946); Section 92(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935; Section 4 of the India (Central Government and Legislature) Act, 1946; and Sections 9 and 19 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
sections.argument: The appellant contended that the Essential Supplies Act was not validly extended to the District of Darjeeling and was not therefore in force there on the date of the alleged offence.
sections.analysis: As the Governor's notification extended the Act to the District of Darjeeling without specifying any particular period for its applicability, the Act would remain in force in that district as long as it remained in force in the rest of India, and a fresh notification of the Governor under section 92(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, was not necessary. Under the adaptations made under sections 9 and 19 of the Indian Independence Act, the powers conferred on the Houses of Parliament became vested in the Constituent Assembly. Furthermore, there was no question of delegation of legislative power as the Legislature had itself applied its mind and fixed the duration of the Act, leaving only the machinery to reach the maximum period to be worked out in a particular manner.
sections.judgement: The Act was held to be validly in force in the District of Darjeeling on the date of the alleged contravention.

sections.facts: The Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 came into operation in the city of Poona on 15th of February, 1950. In 1957, the Corporation, in order to boost industrial development and encourage industrialists to establish industries in the city, decided to give concessions in the nature of exemption from octroi duty and made rule 62 B in Chapter VIII to the Schedule of the Act, under which no octroi was to be levied for twelve years in an demarcated 'Industrial Estate or Area'. Later, the Corporation framed extensive new octroi Rules under its resolution dated 7th August, 1962, wherein Rule 5(8) provided for octroi exemption. The Corporation levied octroi on materials received by the appellants, and their applications for exemption under rule 5(8) were rejected on the ground that the area within which their concerns were situated had not been declared and demarcated as an industrial area. Aggrieved, the appellants filed petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for a writ of Mandamus requiring the Corporation to demarcate the area and grant exemption. During the pendency of the petitions, rule 5(8) was repealed. The appellants amended their writ petitions to contend that the repeal of rule 5(8) was illegal and ultra vires, and alternatively that they were entitled to the benefit of unrepealed rule 62 B. The High Court dismissed the petitions, holding that both rules were repealed without legal flaw, and that on merits the area had not been demarcated as an industrial estate, which was solely in the discretion of the Corporation.
sections.statute: Section 127(2) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 authorised the Corporation to impose octroi and other taxes, while section 149 prescribed the procedure to be followed in levying taxes. Rule 62 B in Chapter VIII to the Schedule of the Act and Rule 5(8) of the new octroi Rules provided for exemption from octroi duty in demarcated industrial areas. Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 and Articles 14 and 226 of the Constitution of India were also invoked.
sections.argument: In the appeals to this Court, the appellants contended: (1) that the disputed area had been included in the development plan under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 before the promulgation of rule 5(8) and had thus automatically become an industrial estate or area for the purposes of that rule; (2) that the Corporation had refused to grant exemption to the appellants on the arbitrary ground that the concern of the appellants was not a new one; (3) that there was a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as some industries in similar situations had been granted exemption while the appellants were deprived of the benefit of rule 5(8); and (4) that while denying the benefit of rule 5(8), the Corporation had taken into consideration extraneous or irrelevant considerations.
sections.analysis: No area had been declared as an industrial area under the development plan before 1957; the disputed area became an industrial area under the Bombay Town Planning Act only after the enforcement of the development plan on 15th August, 1966. A bare perusal of rule 5(8) makes it apparent that an industrial estate or area means the area demarcated by the Corporation from time to time for the purpose of the rule; therefore, demarcation under the Town Planning Act is not demarcation for the purpose of rule 5(8), and without such demarcation exemption cannot be claimed. The purpose of the Town Planning Act is to plan the town and keep industrial areas away from residential or commercial areas, whereas the purpose of demarcation under rule 5(8) is to give incentives and impetus to industries in a particular area. Furthermore, the preamble to the new octroi Rules makes it clear that rule 62 B was repealed by necessary implication because octroi was made the subject matter of an exhaustive new set of rules covering the entire field, including exemptions. Finally, the considerations that weighed with the Corporation in denying the exemption cannot be said to be irrelevant or extraneous, as they fall within the ambit of rule 5(8).
sections.judgement: The appeals were dismissed.

sections.facts: The second defendant sold property belonging to himself and his minor son, the third defendant, and also executed an indemnity bond in favour of the vendee agreeing to indemnify him for any loss that might be caused in case the sale of the third defendant's half share should later on be set aside. The vendee sold the property to the plaintiffs and assigned the indemnity bond in their favour, and the plaintiffs took possession of the property. The third defendant, after attaining majority, sued for setting aside the sale in respect of his half share and for partition. The plaintiffs contested the suit, but the third defendant's suit was decreed; he, however, did not dispossess the plaintiffs. Meanwhile, a creditor of the third defendant obtained a money decree against him and, in execution thereof, attached and brought to sale the third defendant's half share. The brother-in-law of the plaintiffs purchased the property, but the plaintiffs continued in possession. Thereafter, the plaintiffs filed a suit for recovery of half the consideration paid by them. The trial court decreed the suit, but the High Court, on appeal, confined the decree to the actual loss sustained, namely, the amount for the court sale and the amount spent for the defence of the third defendant's suit. The appeal was brought before the Court on the question of the quantum of damages to which the plaintiffs were entitled.
sections.argument: The plaintiffs filed the suit on the allegation that they sustained damage by the loss of one half of the property bought by them and were entitled to recover damages from the second defendant. The suit was contested on the ground that the court sale in favour of the brother-in-law of the plaintiffs was benami for the plaintiffs, and that as the plaintiffs never lost ownership or possession of the half share, they did not sustain any loss.
sections.analysis: The sale of the half share of the third defendant was not void ab initio but was only voidable. In such a case, the indemnity bond becomes enforceable only if the vendee is dispossessed from the properties, because a breach of the covenant can only occur on the disturbance of the vendee's possession. So long as the vendee remains in possession, he suffers no loss and no suit can be brought for damages either on the basis of the indemnity bond or for the breach of a covenant of the warranty of title.
sections.judgement: The High Court was right in granting a decree to the plaintiffs only for the sum which was the actual loss sustained by them.

sections.facts: A settlement was arrived at on 22.2.1972 between the Rajasthan State Electricity Board and the Union representing its employees. In pursuance of this settlement, a notification dated 22.3.1972 was issued revising the pay scales of various categories of posts, effective from 1st April, 1969, under which Meter Reader/Meter Checker was mentioned under scale No. 3. On December 2, 1972, a Second Settlement was entered into between the parties to remove certain ambiguities, agreeing to have two categories of Meter Readers (Meter Reader I/Meter Checker I and Meter Reader II/Meter Checker II), effective w.e.f. 1.4.1968 and notified on 6.12.1972. Some employees appointed before 6.12.1972 challenged the notification dated 6.12.1972. The Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the notification mainly on the ground that no conciliation proceedings were pending before the settlement, and the Division Bench dismissed the Board's appeal. Accordingly, the Board implemented the judgment and issued orders to provide scale No. 3 to all Meter Readers appointed up to 6.12.1972. During this period, the Board, in exercise of powers under Section 79(c) and (k), framed the Rajasthan State Electricity Board Employees (Emoluments) Regulations, 1978, retrospectively applicable from 1st April, 1974, placing the post of Meter Reader II/Meter Checker II in scale No. 2. In 1979, an arbitration award between the Board and the union again created two categories of Meter Readers/Meter Checkers. Subsequently, 35 employees appointed between 1972–1979 filed writ petitions claiming that since the notification dated 6.12.1972 had been quashed, they were governed by the First Settlement and entitled to pay scale No. 3. The High Court allowed the petitions and granted pay scale No. 3, and the Division Bench dismissed the Board's special appeal. The Board appealed to the Supreme Court against employees appointed after 1.4.1974.
sections.statute: Section 79, sub-sections (c) and (k); Section 19(2).
sections.argument: The contentions of the Board before the Supreme Court were that: (i) even if the earlier High Court decision was final, it only applied to employees appointed before 6th December, 1972; (ii) as regards the present employees, no benefit could be granted as the First Settlement was to remain in force only up to 31st March, 1974; (iii) the appointment orders of the respondents clearly stated they were appointed as Meter Reader/Meter Checkers Gr. II in pay scale No. 2; and (iv) under the Rajasthan State Electricity Employees (Emoluments) Regulations, 1978, applicable from 1st April, 1974, Meter Reader II/Meter Checker II were placed in pay scale No. 2 and Meter Reader I/Meter Checker I in pay scale No. 3. On behalf of the respondent-employees, it was contended that: (i) though according to Clause IX of the First Settlement it was to remain in force till 31st March, 1974, it remained in operation until the expiry of two months from notice of intention to terminate under Section 19(2); (ii) under the 1979 arbitration award two categories were again made, hence all Meter Readers appointed up to 1979 before the award were entitled to scale No. 3; and (iii) the contentions regarding the expiration of the first settlement and the Regulations were rightly negatived by the Division Bench as they were not taken in the writ petitions or argued before the Single Judge.
sections.analysis: The respondents sought to take advantage of the First Settlement merely because it did not mention Grade I or II and provided pay scale No. 3 for Meter Reader/Meter Checker. This ambiguity was clarified by an agreement between the Board and the Union on 2.12.1972 to place Meter Reader/Meter Checker in two different grades, after which there was no restriction on the Board to appoint Meter Readers/Meter Checkers in Grade II after 1.4.1974. Furthermore, the appointment orders specifically stated that respondents were appointed as Meter Readers/Meter Checkers Gr. II in pay scale No. 2, and respondents could not show that the Board lacked the power to make such appointments. Even if the High Court had quashed the second settlement, the Board's stand that the first settlement was clarified by the second was at least sufficient notice within the meaning of Section 19(2) that the Board had terminated the first settlement after 31.3.1974. Additionally, the Rajasthan State Electricity Board (Emoluments) Regulations, 1978 were made in exercise of powers conferred by Section 79, sub-sections (c) and (k).
sections.judgement: Appeals allowed.

sections.facts: The four appellants along with seven other accused were tried under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The Trial Court convicted eight accused, including the four appellants, under Section 302/149 I.P.C. and awarded life imprisonment, while convicting Appellants Nos. 1, 2, and 4 under Section 147 I.P.C. to one year's R.I. and Appellant No. 3 under Section 148 I.P.C. to two years' R.I. Three accused were acquitted by the Trial Court for want of corroboration. On appeal, the High Court upheld the convictions of the four appellants on all counts and acquitted the other four co-accused for want of corroboration.
sections.statute: Sections 141, 147, 148, 149, and 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
sections.argument: The appellants contended that Appellants Nos. 3 and 4 should also be acquitted for want of corroboration, given that the Trial Court acquitted three accused and the High Court acquitted four accused on that basis. The State countered that under Section 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C., corroboration regarding individual accused was not necessary, and there was sufficient corroboration on record to establish that the accused were members of the unlawful assembly at the time of the offence.
sections.analysis: Section 149 creates a specific and distinct offence imposing constructive or vicarious criminal liability on members of an unlawful assembly for acts committed in prosecution of its common object, which must fall within Section 141 I.P.C. Overt acts or active participation by every person are not necessary; mere membership with the requisite common object or knowledge fastens liability. Once it is established that the accused formed an unlawful assembly and an offence was committed in prosecution of its common object, every member is guilty, and the prosecution need not prove which specific overt act was done by whom. The evidence satisfactorily established that Appellants Nos. 3 and 4 were members of the unlawful assembly at the relevant time, rendering it immaterial whether they actively participated or caused specific injuries. The High Court erred in acquitting co-accused on the grounds of non-participation in violent acts or lack of corroboration, as courts cannot afford to be charitable in undeserving criminal cases.
sections.judgement: Appeal dismissed.

sections.facts: The appellant company could not work its Mills to full capacity owing to short supply of sugarcane and got the permission of the Government to sell its machinery but continued crushing cane under a lease from the purchaser. The workmen's Union in order to frustrate the transaction resolved to go on strike and communicated its resolution to the company. There was correspondence between the parties in course of which the company offered to pay to the workmen 25 per cent. of the profits of the sale on condition that the strike notice must immediately be withdrawn. The workmen did not fulfill the condition and made certain counter proposals. The company insisted that the condition must first be fulfilled before the counter proposals could be considered and renewed its offer. Although the workmen did not actually go on strike, they did not withdraw the strike notice, and did not cooperate with the management in the dismantling and delivery of the machinery to the purchaser, with the result that the company lost heavily. On the expiry of the lease and closure of the industry, the services of the workmen were duly terminated by the company on March 21, 1951. The workmen thereafter claimed the share of profits on the basis of the offer made by the company in the correspondence, and the dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication by the U.P. Government by a notification under section 3 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act of 1947. The Tribunal held that the company was bound by the offer it had made and awarded a sum of Rs. 45,000 to the workmen as representing their share of the profits. On appeal, the award of the Industrial Tribunal was affirmed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal.
sections.statute: Section 3 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act XXVIII of 1947, and the definition of an industrial dispute contained in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act XIV of 1947 as adopted by the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act XXVIII of 1947.
sections.argument: It was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the notification was ultra vires, and the reference and the award void in consequence, and that there having been no concluded agreement between the parties, it was not bound to pay.
sections.analysis: The definition of an industrial dispute contained in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act XIV of 1947 and adopted by the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act XXVIII of 1947 contemplated the existence of an industry and a subsisting relationship of employer and employee between the parties; therefore, there could be no industrial dispute within the meaning of those Acts where the industry had been closed, and the closure was real and bona fide, if the dispute arose on such closure, or thereafter, if that could be conceived. Section 3 of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act of 1947 only required that there must be an industrial dispute before the Government could make a reference under that section, and consequently, in the instant case where the claim in dispute had arisen, if at all, prior to the closing of the industry, the Government was fully competent to issue the notification. In the instant case, however, as the findings of the Tribunal were inconsistent and conflicting, the Court examined the correspondence and held that it did not establish that there was a concluded agreement between the parties whereby the workmen could be entitled to any share of the profits. Nor was the award sustainable as one for compensation for termination of the services of workmen on closure of the industry, as such discharge was different from discharge on retrenchment, which implied the continuance of the industry and discharge only of the surplusage, and the workmen were not entitled either under the law as it stood on the day of their discharge or even on merits to any compensation.
sections.judgement: Consequently, the award made by the Labour Appellate Tribunal must be set aside.

sections.facts: The petitioner, an association of dealers engaged in the business of selling dry fruit in North India, who purchase dry fruits either locally or through imports from outside India, challenged the grant of additional licences to the respondent diamond exporters.
sections.statute: Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
sections.argument:
On behalf of the petitioners, it was contended: (i) that the goods sought to be imported on the Additional Licences included those which were prohibited by the prevalent Import Policy; (ii) that the principle which was applied to the import of acrylic easter monomers extends likewise to the import of all other commodities under Additional Licences granted to diamond exporters in similar circumstances and, therefore, the diamond exporters are not entitled to import dry fruit; and (iii) that the import of dry fruit is covered by item 121 in Appendix 2 Part B (List of Restricted Items) of the Import Policy 1985-88 and, therefore, the respondents are not entitled to resort to Item 1 of Appendix 6.

On behalf of the respondents, it was contended: (i) that paragraph 176 of the Import Policy 1978-79 envisages the grant of Additional Licences for the import of raw materials which have been placed on Open General Licence for Actual Users (Industrial); (ii) that they import the dry fruits as raw material for the purpose of selling to eligible Industrial Actual Users for processing for manufacturing into a variety of products under Item 1 of Appendix 6 of the Import Policy 1985-86; (iii) that item 121 of Appendix 2 Part B (List of Restricted Items) is not attracted because it refers to "consumer goods", and consumer goods are not raw material for the purposes of item 1 of Appendix 6; and (iv) that the petition under Article 32 is not maintainable because the petitioners' fundamental rights are not violated, in as much as no appeal has been filed by the Customs Authorities or by the Import Control Authorities against the interim order dated January 8, 1986 of the High Court directing the Customs Authorities to permit the respondents to clear the imported consignment of almonds.
sections.analysis:
Under the Import Policy 1978-79, dry fruits (excluding cashewnuts) could be imported by all persons for whatever purpose under the Open General Licence, and no Additional Licence was required. By wrongful denial of Additional Licence to diamond exporters no damage can be said to have been suffered by them and no question of restitution could arise; the wrongful denial was wholly immaterial to the importing of dry fruits (excluding cashewnuts). The respondents have not shown that dry fruits were placed on Open General Licence specifically for Actual Users (Industrial), as their import was open to all persons.

Under the Import Policy 1985-88, dry fruits (excluding cashewnuts and dates) are no longer open to import under Open General Licence. If regarded as items for stock and sale, their import is governed by paragraph 181(3) in Chapter XIII of the Import Policy 1985-88, which allows import against licences issued to dealers engaged in this trade. The diamond exporters cannot be regarded as dealers engaged in the trade of stocking and selling dry fruits (excluding cashewnuts and dates) and are not entitled to the advantage of paragraph 181(3).

Dry fruits must be regarded as consumer goods of agricultural origin, with "agricultural origin" used in the broadest sense. They do not appear in Appendix 3 Part A and 5 nor can they be imported under Open General Licence under the Import Policy 1985-88. Inasmuch as they fall within item 121 of Appendix 2 Part B, they are excluded from the scope of item 1 of Appendix 6 and cannot be imported as raw materials and consumables for sale to Actual Users (Industrial). "Consumer goods" in item 121 of Appendix 2 Part B can refer to dry fruits imported for supply to Actual Users (Industrial).

The expression "specifically banned" occurring in the Court's order dated April 18, 1985 determines the range of items open to import by diamond exporters holding Additional Licences. Present Appendix 2 Part A and Appendix 2 Part B together constitute what was originally List 4 (List of Absolutely Banned Items) under the Import Policy 1978-79. Diamond exporters holding Additional Licences were not entitled to import goods enumerated in Appendix 2 Part B of the Import Policy 1985-88, and thus cannot take advantage of item 121 of Appendix 2 Part B to import dry fruits. Furthermore, holders of Additional Licences are entitled to import only goods included in Appendix 6 Part 2 List 8 of the Import Policy 1985-88, which does not include dry fruits. They are also not entitled to the benefit extended to diamond exporters who had imported items under irrevocable Letters of Credit opened and established before October 18, 1985.

Finally, an interim order cannot defeat the fundamental rights of the petitioners merely because it has not been questioned by the Customs Authorities or the Import Control Authorities.
sections.judgement: Allowing the Writ Petition and the Appeal, respondents Nos. 10 and 11 are restrained from importing dry fruits during the period 1985-88 under the Additional Licences granted to them under the Import Policy 1978-79.

sections.facts: Initially the appellant was a 100% subsidiary of the British company, Crompton Parkinson Ltd. In 1947 an agreement called "Technical Aid Agreement" was concluded between the two companies under which the appellant agreed to pay to the parent company 5% of the net value of its sales every year as service fee for the use of their patterns, valuable designs, technical aid, benefit of research and ancillary services and facilities. As the appellant obtained the benefit of the parent company's technical knowledge and research it did not maintain a separate research establishment on which it would otherwise have had to spend far more than the service fee it paid. The agreement had received the approval of the Government; the income tax authorities had, every year, allowed the service fee as legitimate expenditure; and the remittances to the parent company had been sanctioned by the Reserve Bank of India. In the claim for bonus by the workmen, the Tribunal, in calculating the gross profits, pruned down the allowable expenditure on account of the service fee to one fourth on the grounds that the amount of service fee paid was excessive and beyond the requirements of commercial necessity and that a large part of the payment was in the nature of capital expenditure. In calculating the available surplus the Tribunal deducted as a first charge 4 1/2 months basic wages as bonus before deducting depreciation and income tax contrary to the terms of the Full Bench formula.
sections.analysis: Unless it was definitely found that a purported expenditure was sham or had been made with the express object of minimising the profits with a view to deprive the workmen of their bonus, the Tribunal could not substitute its own judgment as to what was or was not commercially justified in place of that of the appellant and its directors. The service fee was a genuine expenditure and represented a binding contractual obligation which could legally be enforced against the appellant and a breach thereof may have had serious consequences affecting its business. Such departures from the Full Bench Formula by Tribunals were to be deprecated.
sections.judgement: Held, that the entire amount of service fee paid ought to have been allowed as proper expenditure. Held further, that the Tribunal acted wrongly in deducting bonus as a prior charge even before the recognised items of prior charges. Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Its Workmen, C.A. Nos. 459 and 460 of 1957, decided on 5 5 59, followed.

sections.facts: The Madhya Pradesh Government issued a notification under section 5(2) of the Minimum Wages Act (II of 1948), prescribing the minimum rates of wages for employment in stone breaking and stone crushing operations carried on in mines in exercise of the authority delegated to it by the President by a notification under article 258 of the Constitution. The appellant company, engaged in the manganese mining industry, challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition filed in the High Court. The High Court found against the appellant and rejected the petition.
sections.statute: Section 5(2) and Section 27 of the Minimum Wages Act (II of 1948); Item 8 in Part 1 of the Schedule to the Act; Article 258 of the Constitution.
sections.argument: The appellant's case was that the said notification was ultra vires section 5(2) of the Act.
sections.analysis: The question for determination in the appeal was whether item 8 in Part 1 of the Schedule to the Act, properly construed, included stone breaking and stone crushing operations in a mining industry. Item 8 in Part 1 of the Schedule to the Act was not intended to cover the breaking or crushing of stones incidental to mining operations and must be limited to stone breaking and stone crushing employment in quarries. It would, however, be open to the Government, if it so desired, to achieve the object it had in view in issuing the impugned notification by adding appropriate items to the Schedule in exercise of its power under section 27 of the Act. Furthermore, it was not necessary for the appellant to challenge the vires of the Presidential notification in the first instance in order that he might impugn the notification in question (A. Thangal Kunju Musaliar v. M. Venkitachalam Potti, referred to).
sections.judgement: Held, that the impugned notification was ultra vires section 5(2) of the Act and could not be enforced.

sections.facts: The State Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the Essential Commodities Act as delegated to it by the Notification GSR 800 dated June 9, 1978 made the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Commodities Dealers (Licensing and Distribution) Order, 1982 after obtaining prior concurrence of the Central Government. This order sought to regulate the sale and purchase of scheduled commodities as specified in schedule I to the Order, which included edible oil seeds and edible oil. The State Government issued a circular order dated June 21, 1985, containing directions regulating the transport and export of groundnut seeds and oil outside the State, permitting oil millers and traders to export oil and groundnut seeds only on the condition that they deliver oil to the State Government at a fixed price in proportion of one tonne of oil for every three tonnes to be transported outside the State, with similar conditions imposed in respect of groundnut seeds, requiring them to execute undertakings. The respondents, who were oil millers and traders carrying on business in the sale and purchase of groundnut seed and groundnut oil, challenged the validity of the 1982 Order and the 1985 Circular in writ petitions to the High Court. A Single Judge quashed the order of the State Government on the findings that the directions violated Articles 19(1)(g) and 301. On appeal by the State Government, a Division Bench held that the order was violative of section 3(2)(f), section 3(3B) and section 3(5) of the Act as the directions amounted to imposition of levy without prior concurrence of the Central Government, and were outside the purview of the State Government under clause 12 of the 1982 Order, recording no finding on Article 301.
sections.statute: The Essential Commodities Act is a Central Enactment providing for the control of the production, supply and distribution, trade and commerce in certain specified essential commodities. Section 3 of the Act confers power on the Central Government to provide for regulating or prohibiting the production, supply and distribution thereof and trade and commerce therein, if it is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supply of any essential commodities or of securing their equal distribution and availability on fair price. The Central Government issued Notification No. GSR 800 dated June 9, 1978 delegating its powers under section 3(1) of the Act to the State Governments to make orders in respect of matters specified in various sub-clauses of sub-section (2) of section 3 in relation to foodstuffs subject to conditions specified therein. By clause (2) of the Notification, the Central Government expressly placed restrictions on the State Government relating to matters specified in clauses (a), (c), (d) and (f) of sub-section (2) of section 3, requiring that the State Government obtain prior concurrence of the Central Government.
sections.argument: In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the directions contained in the Government Order dated 21st June, 1985 were issued by the State Government in exercise of its powers under clause 12(2) of the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Commodities Dealers (Licensing and Distribution) Order, 1982 which had been made by the State Government with the prior concurrence of the Central Government in exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of the Act, and that the directions were legal and valid.
sections.analysis: The directions contained in the Government Circular Order dated June 21, 1985 are illegal and void as the same have been issued in contravention of the power delegated to the State Government under Notification No. GSR 800 dated June 9, 1978. The 1982 Order does not contain any provision placing any restriction on the transport or movement of edible oil or oil seeds, nor does it provide for imposition of compulsory levy or fix any price. The directions placing restrictions on the movement of oil seeds and oil, imposing compulsory levy, and requiring millers and traders to sell oil seeds and oil at a price fixed by the State Government are outside the purview of the 1982 Order and have no sanction of law. If the State Government was facing any problem, it could have made amendments to the 1982 Order regulating matters specified in clauses (d) and (f) of section 3(2) of the Act after obtaining prior concurrence of the Central Government, but no such course was followed. The directions requiring sales to the State Government fall directly within section 3(2)(f) of the Act, and the State Government had no authority to place such restrictions without prior concurrence. The purpose of obtaining prior concurrence is to ensure availability of essential commodities throughout the country; State Governments are not authorised to impose restrictions on movement as it reflects on price and availability in other States, and the Central Government must balance the interests of various States. A delegate is not entitled to exercise powers in excess or in contravention of delegated powers; any order issued in excess is illegal and void. The power under clause 12(1) of the 1982 Order to issue instructions is limited to the subject matter of the 1982 Order. What could not be done directly could not be permitted to be done indirectly by virtue of clause 12 of the 1982 Order, the scope and ambit of which did not authorise the State Government to impose the restrictions.
sections.judgement: The High Court has rightly struck down the directions issued by the State Government. The appeals are dismissed.

sections.facts: The criminal complaint instituted by the appellant was taken cognizance of by the Magistrate for offences under sections 494, 496, 498 A, 112, 114, 120, 120 B and 34 IPC. It was alleged that the first respondent had married the second respondent while the proceedings for decree of divorce were still pending, and that the marriage was performed secretly in the presence of respondent Nos. 3 to 6. The High Court, however, on the application of the first respondent quashed the proceedings before the Magistrate.
sections.statute: Sections 494, 496, 498 A, 112, 114, 120, 120 B and 34 of the Indian Penal Code; Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
sections.analysis: The High Court was in error in assessing the material before it and concluding that the complaint cannot be proceeded with. In proceedings instituted on complaint, exercise of the inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the High Court to quash the proceedings is called for only in cases where the complaint does not disclose any offence or is frivolous, vexatious or oppressive. It is not necessary that there should be a meticulous analysis of the case before the trial to find out whether the case would end in conviction or not; the complaint has to be read as a whole. In the instant case, there were specific allegations in the complaint disclosing the ingredients of the offence taken cognizance of, and it was for the complainant to substantiate the allegations by evidence at a later stage. In the absence of circumstances to hold prima facie that the complaint was frivolous, there was no justification for the High Court to interfere.
sections.judgement: Appeal by special leave allowed.

sections.facts: The Punjab Government acquired certain parcels of land belonging to two brothers L and N who refused to accept the compensation offered to them and applied to the Government of Punjab under r. 6 of the Punjab Land Acquisition (Defence of India) Rules, 1943, to refer to arbitration their joint claim based on the allegation that the land belonged to them jointly. The State Government referred the matter to an arbitrator as required under r. 10 who passed an award in favour of both L and N ordering inter alia payment of an amount higher than what was offered to them by the Government. The Government appealed against the said award to the High Court. During the pendency of the appeal before the High Court, respondent L died, and as no application for bringing on record his legal representative had been made within the time limit, the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appeal had abated against L and that its effect was that the appeal against N also abated.
sections.statute: Order 22 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure; Rules 6 and 10 of the Punjab Land Acquisition (Defence of India) Rules, 1943.
sections.analysis: There can be no question of abatement of appeal against the co-respondents of the deceased respondent as Order 22 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not provide for the same, but in certain circumstances the appeal cannot proceed against them and such a result depends on the nature of the relief sought in the appeal. If the Court can deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interest of the appellant and the respondents other than the deceased respondent, it has to proceed with the appeal and decide it; otherwise it will have to refuse to proceed further with the appeal and therefore dismiss it. Ordinarily, the consideration which will weigh with the court in deciding upon the question whether the entire appeal had abated or not will be whether the appeal between the appellants and the respondents other than the deceased respondent can be said to be properly constituted or can be said to have all the necessary parties for the decision of the controversy before the court. The tests to determine this are: (a) when the success of the appeal may lead to the court's coming to a decision which will be in conflict with the decision between the appellant and the deceased respondent, thereby leading to contradictory decrees with respect to the same subject matter; (b) when the appellant could not have brought the action for the necessary relief against those respondents alone who are still before the court; and (c) when the decree against the surviving respondents, if the appeal succeeds, would be ineffective, that is to say, it could not be successfully executed. The abatement of an appeal against the deceased respondent means not only that the decree between the appellant and the deceased respondent has become final, but also as a necessary corollary that the appellate court cannot in any way modify that decree directly or indirectly. When the decree in favour of the respondents is joint and indivisible, the appeal against the respondents other than the deceased respondent cannot be proceeded with if the appeal against the deceased respondent has abated.
sections.judgement: In the present case, the appeal against N alone was not properly constituted when the appeal against L had abated, and the State appeal against N alone could not proceed.

sections.facts: Notices under section 22(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922, were not complied with by the respondent (assessee), and the Income tax Officer issued notices under section 22(4). Since they were also not complied with, the Income tax Officer made a best judgment assessment under section 23(4). The assessee applied under section 27 for reopening the assessment. The Income tax Officer found sufficient cause for noncompliance with notices under section 22(4), but declined to reopen the assessment as there was no sufficient cause for noncompliance with notices under section 22(2). This order was confirmed in appeal and by the Tribunal, but the High Court held in favour of the assessee.
sections.analysis: Under section 23(4), on the assessee committing any of the defaults mentioned therein—namely, failure to make a return required by notice under section 22(2) or a revised return under section 22(3), noncompliance with terms of a notice under section 22(4), or failure to comply with terms of a notice under section 23(2)—the Income tax Officer is bound to make a best judgment assessment. Section 27 empowers the Income tax Officer to cancel the assessment when sufficient cause is shown, but such cause must be shown for each default. Therefore, if the assessee defaults by not filing a return pursuant to section 22(2) and also fails to comply with a notice under section 22(4), sufficient cause must be shown for noncompliance with both provisions. The Legislature could not have intended that in cases of multiple defaults, each warranting an ex parte best judgment assessment, an assessee could obtain cancellation by showing cause for only one such default.
sections.judgement: The view taken in Chiranjilal Tibrewala vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City II, was approved, deciding the appeal in favour of the appellant.

sections.facts: The assessee encashed 51 high denomination notes of Rs. 1,000 each in January 1946. In his application for encashment, the assessee explained that as a colliery proprietor and contractor, he required large sums to meet emergencies and make weekly labour payments of about Rs. 30,000 to Rs. 40,000, and that the sum of Rs. 51,000 realized by encashment was not profit but floating capital for conducting business. The Income-tax Officer rejected this explanation, treated the amount as profit from an undisclosed source, and assessed it as assessable income.
sections.argument: The assessee contended that the burden lay on the Department to establish that the amount in question was income liable to tax, and that the Department had failed to establish this.
sections.analysis: It was not correct that the assessee was not required to prove anything and that the burden lay entirely upon the Department to prove that the amount received from encashment was income. Where an entry in the account books shows receipt of a sum or conversion of notes by the assessee, the assessee must establish the source of the money and prove it is not of an income nature; the Department is not required to prove anything at this initial stage. If the assessee's business, state of accounts, and dealings demonstrate that he might reasonably have kept the whole or part of the sum in high denomination notes for convenience, the initial burden is prima facie discharged, and the Department cannot unreasonably reject that explanation. However, if the explanation is unconvincing, the Department may reject it and infer that the amount represents income from disclosed or undisclosed sources, provided it shows an inherent weakness in the explanation or rebuts it with information or evidence in its possession. The receipt of money or conversion of notes is itself prima facie evidence against the assessee in the absence of a satisfactory explanation. In the present case, although cash was received from banks and sent between various places of business, no central account of such transfers was disclosed. There was no account of personal expenses, and the assessee failed to prove why such large sums were kept on hand at one place when banks existed at each workplace where he held accounts. Furthermore, despite keeping this large sum on hand, further cheques were drawn to meet current needs while this amount remained untouched.
sections.judgement: Held that the Department was justified in holding that the amount of Rs. 51,000 was assessable income of the assessee from some undisclosed source.

sections.facts: The appellant's election to the State Assembly was set aside by the High Court on the ground of corrupt practice falling under section 123(5) of the Representation of People Act. It was alleged that the appellant hired and procured vehicles for the free conveyance of voters, which was denied by the appellant. The High Court allowed amendment of the election petition by inserting a new sub-paragraph 12(d), stating that the names of the persons who hired or procured the vehicles for carrying the voters to the polling station were given in schedule III(i) of the petition, on the view that the information given was a necessary particular to allege and prove that the vehicle was used for the conveyance of the voters.
sections.statute: Section 83 and Section 123(5) of the Representation of People Act.
sections.argument: It was contended in this Court: (i) that the tractor in which the voters were alleged to have been carried to the polling station was taken there in some other connection and that though the tractor was in the name of his wife as benamidar, it really belonged to the appellant and, as such, no question of hiring or procuring it, whether on payment or otherwise, arose so as to make it fall within the purview of section 123(5) of the Act; and (ii) that the High Court had committed a serious error of law in allowing the election petition to be amended after the expiry of the period prescribed for its presentation.
sections.analysis: (1) (a) There is no justification for contending that there could be no question or occasion for hiring or procuring the tractor because it belonged to the appellant. It cannot be urged that the tractor, which belonged to his wife, must be deemed to belong to the appellant or that it should be inferred that she was a mere benamidar when that was not the appellant's case anywhere. The tractor belonged to the wife of the appellant and was not his own property. (b) It would amount to "procuring" the tractor if it could be shown that the appellant obtained or got or acquired the tractor from his wife. The dictionary meaning of the word "procure" is "to obtain as by request loan effort, labour; get, gain, come into possession of". This is the correct meaning of the word used in section 123(5). (c) It is not always possible for an election petitioner to adduce direct evidence to prove that a particular vehicle was hired or procured by the candidate or his agent or by any other person with the consent of the candidate or his election agent, but this can be inferred from the proved circumstances where such inference is justifiable. (2) It is futile to contend that a new corrupt practice was allowed to be inserted by the High Court's order of amendment. The schedule was an integral part of the election petition and the original election petition contained what was required to be stated by section 83 of the Act and the amendment was meant to furnish some further particulars in regard to the same corrupt practice. When issue No. 2 was framed by the High Court, the appellant was fully aware that the election petitioners had alleged the user of the vehicles also and that was why he joined issue for the trial of that allegation. (3) There is no obligation on the part of the election petitioners to examine themselves at the trial in the High Court. The evidence which they were able to produce at the trial could not have been rejected for any such fanciful reason when there was nothing to show that the election petitioners were able to give useful evidence to their personal knowledge but stayed away purposely.
sections.judgement: Dismissing the appeal, held that the finding of the High Court that the appellant procured the tractor with trolly and used it for the purpose of transporting the voters to the polling station and thereby committed a corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(5) of the Act is correct.

sections.facts: The respondent was permitted by the Municipal Council to construct a building on the disputed land. Later, the site was reserved under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act for a town planning scheme. When the respondent was prevented from proceeding with the construction, he filed a suit for damages. The Municipal Council, however, by a resolution passed on February 13, 1967 decided to accord permission, after which the suit was withdrawn. The State Government appointed a high power committee to examine the entire matter, and the aforesaid resolution was rescinded by the Municipal Council. The respondent made a fresh application in July, 1968, which was kept in abeyance, leading him to file a writ petition before the High Court in 1969. During the pendency of the case, the Municipal Council passed a resolution on June 29, 1970 deciding to replan the scheme with respect to the area in question in accordance with the recommendations of the high power committee. The High Court by its judgment dated April 18, 1972 directed the Municipal Council to dispose of the application in accordance with law. The Municipal Council, however, by its order dated November 21, 1972 rejected it on the basis of the 1970 resolution. In the writ application challenging the rejection, the High Court allowed the writ petition on the basis of constructive res judicata.
sections.statute: Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act.
sections.argument: In the writ application, the respondent contended that the disputed question must be deemed to have been finally settled in his favour in view of the earlier judgment which was binding on the parties by reason of the rule of res judicata, whereas the State contended that no final decision was arrived at in the earlier case. In the appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the previous judgment could not be interpreted as a direction commanding the Municipal Council to allow the proposed construction, and that the plots were urgently needed for providing parking space for vehicles. For the respondent, it was contended that the resolution of February 13, 1967 was passed by way of a compromise between the parties and acting thereupon he withdrew his suit, making it binding on the Municipal Council, and that the 1970 resolution should be completely ignored without allowing the Municipal Council to bypass the High Court's judgment.
sections.analysis: The resolution dated February 13, 1967 was not binding on the Municipal Council so as to disable it from taking a different decision later, as it was not the result of a compromise between the parties. At best for the respondent, it could be assumed that when the resolution was passed the acquisition of the land was not so urgently essential as to call for his dispossession, but for that reason it could not be said that the plots had become immune from being utilised for any other public purpose forever. The question of whether a particular scheme framed under statutory provisions is in the public interest must be determined according to the need of the time, and a final decision for all times cannot be taken; schemes may need modification or substitution as community requirements vary with evolving social life. A body like the Municipal Council entrusted with public duty must assess the situation from time to time and vary the scheme to meet changing public needs. Furthermore, the high power committee had reported that the land was needed for proper circulation of traffic. There was no scope for the application of res judicata, as the High Court's judgment dated April 18, 1972 did not finally decide the controversy and left it open for the Municipal Council to reconsider and dispose of the respondent's application in accordance with law.
sections.judgement: The appeal was allowed.

sections.facts: The appellant was the intermediary in respect of vast forest and other lands in the State of Orissa, which vested in the State in April 1960 under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951. After the appellant submitted the return for compensation, the Compensation Officer issued an adverse order, and subsequent appeals to the Collector and the Board of Revenue were dismissed. On revision, the High Court set aside the order and remanded the matter. Thereafter, the District Forest Officer made an appraisal of the annual income and submitted it to the Chief Conservator of Forests, who altered and substantially reduced the yield. Both the State and the appellant appealed to the Collector and the Board of Revenue without success. Subsequent revision applications before the High Court led to an order of remand that was challenged in the present appeals before the Supreme Court.
sections.statute: Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951, Sections 26 and 27; Constitution of India, Articles 31(2), 31(3), 31A, and 31B.
sections.argument: The appellant contended that: (1) Interest ought to have been awarded at 12 per cent instead of the statutory rate of 2 1/2 per cent from the date of vesting till payment; (2) Compensation money should be calculated such that its purchasing power on the date of actual payment equals its purchasing power on the date of vesting; (3) The slab system of calculation providing smaller multiples for estates yielding larger incomes is unconstitutional; (4) Because no actual income was derived from the forests during the agricultural year immediately preceding abolition and no income tax was payable, the deduction of income tax from gross assets was illegal; (5) Compensation was not computed in accordance with the scheme of the Act; and (6) The Compensation Officer became functus officio as compensation had not been calculated by the date of vesting.
sections.analysis: Agrarian reform policy aims at extinguishing ancient privileges, where the socio-economic yardstick differs from ordinary commercial transactions, as reflected in Articles 31A and 31B of the Constitution; thus, interest may be notional. Inflationary erosion of currency value does not affect statutory monetary compensation, as the rupee of long ago remains legally equivalent to the rupee of today. Challenges to the adequacy of compensation based on the slab system are barred under Article 31(3) read with Article 31(2) due to Presidential assent. Section 27 relies on assumed, rather than actual, forest income to compute compensation, which equally requires working out and deducting an assumed income tax. Under Section 26, compensation must be calculated on the appraisal of annual yield by a Forest Officer, subject to screening and approval by the Chief Conservator of Forests; the Chief Conservator cannot independently substitute his own appraisal without reference to the Forest Officer's report. Compensation operations are post-statutory exercises, rendering the functus officio argument groundless. Upon remand, the Forest Officer must appraise the annual income and forward the report to the Chief Conservator of Forests, who may approve or modify it before submission to the Compensation Officer.
sections.judgement: Dismissing the appeals, the Supreme Court affirmed the course adopted by the High Court and directed that the proceedings before the Compensation Officer be completed within six months.

sections.facts: Selection to the post of Travelling Ticket Inspector from that of Travelling Ticket Examiner is made by a Selection Board under the Promotion and Selection Rules (Non-Gazetted) framed under the Indian Railway Establishment Code, whereby eligible staff up to four times the number of anticipated vacancies are called for written and viva voce tests under rule 8(7) to prepare a promotional panel. In 1959, in the ex-Muzaffarpur region of the North Eastern Railway, eight vacancies were to be filled immediately and an additional panel of six was to be drawn up. Due to an incorrect assessment, 92 persons, including the appellant, were called for examination instead of 56. A panel of 14 persons was prepared where the appellant was ranked 12th, and in the final list he was ranked 13th, but with an appended note stating that the selection of candidates 9 to 14 was provisional. Subsequently, under the orders of the General Manager as the prescribed authority, the names of candidates 9 to 14 were deleted from the panel. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226, which was dismissed by the High Court.
sections.statute: Article 226 and Article 311 of the Constitution of India; Rule 8(7) of the Promotion and Selection Rules (Non-Gazetted) framed under the Indian Railway Establishment Code.
sections.argument: The appellant contended that the deletion of his name from the panel amounted to a reduction in rank and that the order was bad in law because he was not given an opportunity to be heard before his name was deleted.
sections.analysis: If a civil servant has a right to a particular rank, a reduction from that rank operates as a penalty since he loses the emoluments and privileges of that rank; however, if he has no right to the particular rank, reduction from an officiating higher rank to his substantive lower rank does not ordinarily constitute punishment. Because the word 'provisional' was specifically noted against the appellant's name in the panel, he did not acquire any right to the post. As no penal consequences were visited upon him, the appellant could not complain of any infraction of the constitutional guarantee afforded to government servants, and the deletion of his name from the panel did not attract the provisions of Article 311.
sections.judgement: The deletion of the appellant's name from the panel did not attract the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution, and the appeal against the dismissal of the petition was rejected.

sections.facts: On April 26, 1954, the appellant was arrested for offences under sections 420, 482, 483, 485 and 486 of the Indian Penal Code and bidis alleged to bear counterfeit trade marks were seized from him. On this, a complaint was filed on May 26 against the appellant alleging that he was in possession of counterfeit bidis, wrappers and labels. After investigation, the police submitted a charge sheet on September 30, 1954, and summons was ordered to the appellant on July 22, 1955. The appellant raised a preliminary objection before the Magistrate that the proceedings were barred by section 15 of the Indian Merchandise Marks Act.
sections.statute: Section 15 of the Indian Merchandise Marks Act; Sections 420, 482, 483, 485 and 486 of the Indian Penal Code.
sections.argument: The appellant contended that the offence was discovered on April 26, 1954, when he was arrested and the prosecution which commenced with the issue of process against him on July 22, 1955, was beyond the period of one year provided by section 15.
sections.analysis: It is settled law that unless there is something to the contrary in the statute, when a private complaint is presented it is the date of presentation thereof that marks the commencement of the prosecution. The period of limitation is intended to operate against the complainant and not against the Court. It will defeat the object of the Act and deprive traders of the protection of the law if it were held that the complaint should be thrown out unless process was issued within one year of the discovery of the offence.
sections.judgement: The prosecution was not barred by section 15 as the prosecution commenced on the presentation of the complaint, which was within one year of the discovery of the offence, and not on the issuing of the process.

sections.facts: At an election held on 23rd February, 1986, for the post of Panchayat President, the votes were counted on the 25th February, 1986, and the first respondent was declared elected having secured 649 votes. The petitioner and the second respondent who were the other contestants were declared to have secured only 556 votes and 8 votes respectively, and 55 votes were declared to be invalid votes. Two days after the results were declared i.e. on 27th February, 1986, the petitioner sent telegrams and registered notices alleging irregularities in the counting of the votes, and thereafter he filed an election petition under section 178 of the Tamil Nadu Panchayat Act, 1958. The reliefs claimed in the petition were that the Election Tribunal should set aside the election of the first respondent as the President of the Panchayat, order recounting of votes, and a declaration that the petitioner has been duly elected. The first respondent opposed the election petition and filed a counter statement denying all the allegations contained in the election petition. The Tribunal after recording the evidence of the candidates and the Assistant Returning Officer came to the conclusion that the petitioner was entitled to ask for recount of votes and ordered recounting and called for the ballot papers. In the recount of votes, it was found that there was no difference in the number of votes secured by the petitioner, namely, 556 votes but in so far as the first respondent was concerned he had secured only 528 votes as against the 649 votes he was originally held to have secured. The excess of 121 votes were found to be invalid votes and consequently the total number of invalid votes came to 126 (sic) as against 55 votes originally held to be invalid. There was no difference in the number of 8 votes secured by the third contestant. Based on these figures of the recounting, the Tribunal declined to order re-election and instead declared the petitioner to have been duly elected because the recount clearly proved that the petitioner has secured 28 votes more than the first respondent. Aggrieved by the order of the Election Tribunal, the first respondent filed a Civil Revision Petition in the High Court. A Single Judge allowed the revision petition holding that the Tribunal had erred in ordering a recount of the votes when the petitioner had not made out a prima facie case for an order of recount, observing that the secrecy of the ballot was sacrosanct and should not be violated unless a prima facie case of a compulsive nature had been made out by the defeated candidate. The High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and restored the election result in favour of the first respondent.
sections.statute: Section 178 of the Tamil Nadu Panchayat Act, 1958.
sections.analysis: The right of a defeated candidate to assail the validity of an election result and seek recounting of votes has to be subject to the basic principle that the secrecy of the ballot is sacrosanct in a democracy and hence unless the affected candidate is able to allege and substantiate in acceptable measure by means of evidence that a prima facie case of a high degree of probability existed for the recount of votes being ordered by the Election Tribunal in the interests of justice, a Tribunal or Court should not order the recount of votes. The salutary rule is that the preservation of the secrecy of the ballot is a sacrosanct principle which cannot be lightly or hastily broken unless there is prima facie genuine need for it. The justification for an order for examination of ballot papers and recount of votes is not to be derived from hindsight and by the result of the recount of votes. On the contrary, the justification for an order of recount of votes should be provided by the material placed by an election petitioner on the threshold before an order for recount of votes is actually made. An order of recount of votes must stand or fall on the nature of the averments made and the evidence adduced before the order of recount is made and not from the results emanating from the recount of votes. In the instant case, the petitioner has neither made such averments in the petition nor adduced evidence of such a compulsive nature as could have made the Tribunal reach a prima facie satisfaction that there was adequate justification for the secrecy of ballot being breached.
sections.judgement: Special Leave Petition dismissed.

sections.facts: The Municipalities of Punjab are governed by two enactments: the numerous little ones are statutory bodies created and controlled by the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, and the few large ones by the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976, with the provisions running on identical terms for the purpose of the present petitions. The State of Punjab in April 1977 required the various municipal bodies in the State to impose tax on the sale of Indian made foreign liquor @ Re. 1/- per bottle w.e.f. 20-5-1977. The Municipal authorities having failed to take action pursuant to the directive, the State of Punjab directly issued a notification under section 90(5) of the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976 and a similar provision of the Municipal Act, 1911.
sections.statute: Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976, Section 90, Section 90(2)(b), Section 90(4), and Section 90(5); Punjab Municipal Act, 1911; Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948; and Constitution of India, Articles 14, 19(5), and 265.
sections.argument: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the statutes and the levy on the grounds that: (1) Section 90(2)(b) of the Act suffers from the vice of excessive delegation or legislative abdication, with no guidelines for the exercise of the wide fiscal power of the Corporation or Government, making it too unreasonable to be salvaged by Article 19(5) and too arbitrary to be equal under Article 14. (2) The order imposing the tax itself is vitiated because: (a) it seeks to impose a tax which is already imposed and therefore violates section 90(4); (b) there is double taxation; (c) it levies too heavy taxation; (d) picking out Indian made foreign liquor from the broad spectrum of luxury goods or intoxicants amounts to discrimination; (e) no opportunity of being heard was given; and (f) unequals are being treated equally by imposing Re. 1/- per bottle irrespective of the type of liquor taxed, price of the liquor, and alcoholic content.
sections.analysis:
There is nothing in Article 265 of the Constitution prohibiting double taxation. The plea that a flat rate of Re. 1/- per bottle—be it on brandy or other stronger beverage, or be it Rs. 50/- or Rs. 500/- per bottle—cannot be seriously pressed, as many complex factors enter fixation in the field of taxation and flexibility is necessary for the taxing authority.

If the Municipal body proposes to impose a tax it is required to offer an opportunity to the residents of the area, but no such procedural fetter is found under section 90(5) if the levy is imposed by the State Government; it is impossible for the Court to imply an invitation of objections, and 'no taxation without representation' is not applicable to a Government controlled by an elected legislature exercising taxing power.

Section 90(4) speaks of tax not already imposed. The sales tax imposed by the State Legislature under the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 is no bar to the present levy because Section 90 deals with municipal taxes and the injunction is confined to the repetition of taxes which the Municipality has already imposed under this Act. It is of no moment that another body, including the State Legislature, has entered the field.

While the Founding Document creates the three great instrumentalities and the legislature cannot delegate essential legislative functions, the complexities of modern administration make delegation of some legislative power a compulsive necessity for viability. Control over delegated legislation remains a living continuity as delegates are subject to the principal's authority. Here, taxes levied under the Act can be utilised only for the purposes of the Act, which provides a clear directive regarding the purpose and limit of the tax, and the taxable items are specified. Fixing rates of taxation can be delegated when legislative policy is indicated with sufficient clarity. When imposing taxes for the Municipality, the Government knows what ought to have been done, as the statutory scheme gives it an important role in running municipalities and exercising financial control. Between two interpretations, that which sustains the validity of the law must be preferred.
sections.judgement: Dismissing the appeal. The notification and levy are upheld.

sections.facts: The respondent was assessed to sales tax in the State of Kerala for the year 1962 63 in March, 1964. In December, 1965 the Sales Tax Officer issued notice under R. 33 of the Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Rules, 1950 in force at that time for reopening the original assessment on the ground that certain turnover had escaped assessment. The respondent's objection to the notice having failed it filed a writ petition in the High Court. The learned Single Judge who heard the writ petition felt that it was due to the orders of the court that the Sales tax authorities had been prevented from completing the assessment within the time allowed by Rule 33. While disposing of the writ petition he observed that the Sales Tax Authorities would be at liberty to complete the proceedings initiated by the notice within a further period of 59 days. The respondent preferred an appeal to the division bench which set aside the direction granting 59 days extension for completing the assessment. The Revenue appealed.
sections.statute: According to the relevant portion of Rule 33 of the Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Rules, 1950, the assessing authority "may at any time within three years next succeeding that to which the tax relates determine to the best of his judgment the turnover which has escaped assessment and assess the tax payable on such turnover after issuing a notice to the dealer and after making such enquiry as he considers necessary".
sections.argument: On behalf of the appellant it was contended that on a true construction of Rule 33 it should be held that the proceedings under that rule have to commence within three years next succeeding that to which the tax relates and that it is not necessary that the entire proceedings relating to the escaped assessment should be completed within that period. On behalf of the respondent it was urged that the word 'determine' in Rule 33 meant that the final determination of the turnover which had escaped assessment and the assessment of the tax have to be done within three years.
sections.analysis: In view of the previous decisions of this Court in which provisions similar to Rule 33, namely, sub clauses (2), (4) and (5) of section 11 of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 came up for consideration, the principle is firmly established that assessment proceedings under the Sales Tax Act must be taken to be pending from the time the proceedings are initiated until they are terminated by a final order of assessment. In these cases the initiation of proceedings within the prescribed period was considered sufficient. The fact that the word used in Rule 33 is 'determine' whereas in sections 11(4) and (5) of the Punjab Act the words 'proceed to assess' are used, cannot, in the context of sales tax legislation lead to a different result. The words which follow the word 'determine' in Rule 33 must be accorded their due signification. The words 'assess the tax payable' cannot be ignored and it is clearly meant that the assessment has to be made within the period prescribed. 'Assessment' is a comprehensive word and can denote the entirety of proceedings which are taken with regard to it. It cannot and does not mean a final order of assessment alone unless there is something in the context of a particular provision which compels such a meaning being attributed to it. Rule 33 must not be so interpreted that it may be defeated by taking certain collateral proceedings and obtaining a stay order as was done in the present case or by unduly delaying assessment proceedings beyond a period of three years. It must be interpreted like the analogous provisions considered in earlier cases. This must particularly be so when there is no provision in the Rule in question analogous to sub section (3) of section 34 of the Income tax Act, 1922 by which the Income Tax authorities were debarred from completing the assessment beyond the period prescribed.
sections.judgement: Allowing the appeal.

sections.facts: The appellants were the trustees of a charity fund known as "The Charity Fund founded by Sir Sassoon David, Baronet of Bombay". Clause 13 of the deed of trust, after declaring that the trustees should apply the net income for all or any of the following purposes, namely, (a) the relief and benefit of the poor and indigent members of Jewish or any other community of Bombay or other parts of India or of the world either by making payments to them in cash or providing them with food and clothes and/or lodging or residential quarters or in giving education including scholarships to or setting them up in life or in such other manner as to the said Trustees may seem proper or (b) the institution maintenance and support of hospitals and schools, colleges or other educational institutions or (c) the relief of any distress caused by the elements of nature such as famine, pestilence, fire, tempest, flood, earthquake or any other such calamity or (d) the care and protection of animals useful to mankind or (e) the advancement of religion or (f) other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the foregoing purposes, added by way of provisos: (1) that in applying the net income for the purposes mentioned in sub-cl. (a) the trustees must give preference to the poor and indigent relations or members of the family of Sir Sassoon David, including distant and collateral relatives, and (2) that for the said purpose the trustees must apply not less than half of the income for the benefit of the members of the Jewish community of Bombay only, including the said relatives of Sir Sassoon David and Jewish objects. The question for determination was whether the income from the trust fund was exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act. The High Court concluded that the trust fund could not be said to be held, wholly or partly, for religious or charitable purposes involving an element of public utility and answered the question in the negative.
sections.statute: Section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act.
sections.analysis: There could be no doubt that each one of the primary purposes mentioned in the deed of trust, including the one mentioned in sub-cl. (a), properly construed, involved an element of public utility and thus constituted a valid charitable trust. Although it was open to the trustees to spend the entire income for the purpose mentioned in sub-cl. (a), that could not detract from the validity of the trust since the relations or family members of the founder did not come in directly under any of the other purposes and could do so only under sub-cl. (a) as preferential beneficiaries to be selected from out of the class of primary beneficiaries prescribed by it, in terms of the provisos. The test of the validity of such a public charitable deed of trust should be whether or not at the primary stage of eligibility it could be said to possess that character. In re Koettgan's Will Trusts, applied. Trustees of Gordhandas Govindram Family Charitable Trust vs Commissioner of Income tax (Central), Bombay, [1952] 21 I.T.R. 231, distinguished and held inapplicable. The circumstance that in selecting the actual beneficiaries from the primary class of beneficiaries under sub-cl. (a), the trustees had to give preference under the provisos to the relations or members of the family of Sir Sassoon David, could not therefore affect the public charitable trust constituted under sub-cl. (a).
sections.judgement: The income from the trust properties was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act.

sections.facts: The Respondent Hotel which was also running a Bar for sometime, closed down its business after several years. The Inspectors of the appellant Corporation verified the records of the establishment and reported that at a certain point of time the employment strength of the establishment including the bar was more than 19. Therefore, the establishment was treated as covered provisionally under the Employees State Insurance (ESI) Act, 1948. Since the final date of coverage could be decided only after verifying all the records, the Respondent was asked to produce them. The Respondent did not avail the opportunity afforded to it. Though the Respondent sent its explanation, it was not acceptable to the appellant Corporation and so it passed a detailed order under Section 45A calling upon the Respondent to pay the contribution with interest at 6% failing which it would be recovered as arrears of land revenue. Since this order and the reminder thereto did not evoke any response from the Respondent, the appellant sent a claim in Form 19 to the District Collector requesting him to recover the said amount. The Respondent challenged the proceedings by filing an application under Section 75 of the Act before the ESI Court, which upheld the assessment made by the appellant Corporation, but stated that recovery steps were not justified after the closure of the establishment, and only prosecution as contemplated under Section 85 of the Act was attracted. The appellant Corporation preferred an appeal against the said decision of the ESI Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal and held that since the scheme was made after the closure of the establishment, the appellant was not justified in proceeding against the Respondent. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court, the appellant Corporation preferred the present appeal.
sections.statute: Employees State Insurance (ESI) Act, 1948; Section 26, Section 40, Section 45A, Section 75, and Section 85.
sections.argument: The appellant Corporation contended that so long as the establishment was covered by the provisions of the Act, the Respondent could not circumvent its liability by claiming that before actual recovery proceedings, it had closed down the establishment.
sections.analysis: Admittedly the hotel industry like that of the respondent has been notified by the Government thus extending the provisions of the Act to the hotel industry. Therefore, on the date of commencement of its business, namely, 11.7.85, there was a liability on the Respondent to contribute to the ESI fund. Under Section 40, the primary liability is on the employer to pay, not only his contribution but also the employees' contribution. As such, the employer cannot plead that since he had not deducted the employees' contribution from their wages, he could not be made liable for the same.
